# Psoas abscess

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Wound, soft tissue, bone, and joint infections > Psoas abscess*

[Original Article Link](/library/XI09Yh)

---

## Summary

<u>Psoas</u> <u>abscess</u> (also called <u>iliopsoas</u> <u>abscess</u>) is a rare condition characterized by a localized collection of <u>pus</u> in the <u>iliopsoas muscle</u> compartment. It is categorized into <u>primary psoas abscess</u> (caused by hematogenous or lymphatic spread of a <u>pathogen</u>) and <u>secondary psoas abscess</u> (resulting from contiguous spread from an adjacent infectious focus). The most common causes of <u>secondary psoas abscess</u> are infections of gastrointestinal or musculoskeletal origin. Infections are often monomicrobial, with <u>S. aureus</u> most frequently isolated, followed by <u>E. coli</u>. Polymicrobial <u>abscesses</u> are most commonly of gastrointestinal origin. <u>Computed tomography</u> is the diagnostic modality of choice. <u>Empiric antibiotic therapy</u> should be administered as soon as <u>blood cultures</u> and, if possible, <u>abscess</u> cultures are obtained. A small <u>abscess</u> (< 3.5 cm) in a nonseptic patient can be managed with <u>antibiotic therapy</u> alone. Larger or multiloculated <u>abscesses</u> should be drained under image guidance or with <u>surgery</u>. In a <u>psoas</u> <u>abscess</u> of any kind, the underlying cause should be evaluated and treated.

---

## Etiology

* Primary psoas abscess [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)

* Caused by hematogenous or lymphatic spread of a <u>pathogen</u> from a distant source

* Most often caused by a single <u>pathogen</u>

* <u>Psoas</u> <u>muscle injury</u> (e.g., trauma, <u>ischemia</u>) increases the likelihood of infection. [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)

* More common in Asia and Africa  [[3]](/library/IzYY87)

* Secondary psoas abscess

* Caused by contiguous spread of a <u>pathogen</u> from an adjacent infectious focus

* Primary focus may be: ;  [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)[[4]](/library/r_Yfp7)[[5]](/library/FbbgvH)

* Gastrointestinal: e.g., <u>IBD</u> (especially <u>Crohn disease</u>), <u>colitis</u>, <u>appendicitis</u>, <u>diverticulitis</u>, <u>pancreatitis</u>

* Musculoskeletal: e.g., <u>osteomyelitis</u> (esp. of the <u>vertebrae</u>), <u>Pott disease</u>, paraspinal <u>abscess</u>, <u>septic arthritis</u> (commonly of the hip in children), <u>prosthetic joint infection</u>

* Genitourinary: e.g., <u>pyelonephritis</u>, <u>cystitis</u>

* Cardiovascular: e.g., <u>infective endocarditis</u>, <u>endocarditis</u>, infected aortic endograft

* Postprocedural: e.g., after vascular <u>surgery</u>, <u>arterial catheterization</u>, spinal <u>surgery</u>, instrumentation of the <u>urinary tract</u>

* Different causative pathogens are associated with different primary infectious foci.

* Risk factors for psoas abscess [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)

* <u>Immunodeficiency</u> (e.g., <u>diabetes mellitus</u>, <u>HIV</u>)

* <u>Intravenous drug use</u>

* Trauma

* Causative pathogens [[4]](/library/r_Yfp7)

* Both primary and <u>secondary psoas abscesses</u> are most often monomicrobial.

* Secondary <u>abscesses</u> are more likely to be polymicrobial than primary <u>abscesses</u>.





| Causative pathogens of <u>psoas</u> <u>abscess</u> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Pathogen</u> | Properties |
| <u>S. aureus</u> | <br><br>* Most common causative <u>pathogen</u> [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)<br><br>* Typically associated with a skeletal primary focus<br><br>* <u>Incidence</u> of <u>MRSA</u> is not well established.<br><br><br> |
| <u>E. coli</u> | <br><br>* Second most common causative <u>pathogen</u> [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)<br><br>* Typically associated with gastrointestinal or <u>urinary tract</u> primary focus<br><br><br> |
| <u>Bacteroides</u> spp., <u>S. viridans</u> | <br>* Frequently isolated, especially from a gastrointestinal focus [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)[[4]](/library/r_Yfp7)<br><br> |
| <u>M. tuberculosis</u> | <br><br>* Common causative <u>pathogen</u> in <u>endemic</u> regions of <u>tuberculosis</u> [[6]](/library/O9YInr)<br><br>* More commonly isolated in patients with <u>immunodeficiency</u> [[4]](/library/r_Yfp7)<br><br><br> |

---

## Clinical features

* Classic triad: present in ∼ 30% of cases [[6]](/library/O9YInr)

* <u>Antalgic gait</u>

* <u>Lower back pain</u> (flank <u>pain</u>)

* <u>Fever</u>

* Nonspecific symptoms: lower abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>malaise</u>, weight loss

* Examination findings

* Affected hip lies in a flexed and <u>externally rotated</u> position at rest.

* Passive extension and/or <u>internal rotation</u> of the affected hip elicits <u>pain</u>.

* A tender/nontender mass may be palpable in the <u>ipsilateral</u> iliac or inguinal region.

* Additional features: symptoms related to underlying conditions may be present (e.g., <u>colitis</u>, <u>UTI</u>). [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)

---

## Diagnosis

Imaging is required to confirm the <u>clinical diagnosis</u> of <u>psoas</u> <u>abscess</u>. <u>Laboratory studies</u> provide supportive evidence of an acute infectious process and may be used to monitor response to therapy. Tests to evaluate for a suspected primary focus should be guided by the <u>pretest probability</u> of the underlying etiology, as determined by a thorough history and <u>physical examination</u>. If no obvious primary focus of infection can be identified, the <u>psoas</u> <u>abscess</u> is presumed to be a <u>primary psoas abscess</u>. [[7]](/library/PYbW6H)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u>  [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)[[6]](/library/O9YInr)[[8]](/library/jYb_KH)




* Routine tests for suspected <u>psoas</u> <u>abscess</u>

* <u>CBC</u>: ↑ <u>WBC</u>; <u>anemia</u> may be present

* <u>Inflammatory markers</u>: ↑ <u>ESR</u>, ↑ <u>CRP</u>

* ↑ <u>Creatine kinase</u>

* <u>Procalcitonin</u>: not routinely indicated; usually elevated in patients with <u>sepsis</u>

* <u>Gram stain</u> and culture of blood and <u>abscess</u> <u>aspirate</u>

* A definitive microbiological diagnosis can be made in ∼ 75% of patients. [[4]](/library/r_Yfp7)

* The isolated organism may indicate the primary source of infection (see causative pathogens in ''Etiology'').

* Consider an <u>acid-fast stain</u> (<u>Ziehl-Neelsen stain</u>) and special culture medium if <u>tuberculosis</u> is suspected.

* Tests to evaluate for an underlying etiology 

* <u>Urinalysis</u> and <u>leukocyte esterase</u> in suspected <u>UTI</u>

* <u>HIV serologies</u>/<u>PCR</u> in suspected <u>HIV infection</u>. [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)

* <u>Diagnostic workup for tuberculosis</u> in <u>endemic</u> regions

* <u>Serology</u> for suspected <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u> (see ''Diagnostics'' of <u>ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Obtain <u>blood cultures</u> (and <u>pus</u>/<u>aspirate</u> cultures, if possible) before initiating <u>empiric antibiotic therapy</u>.




### Imaging




#### CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast (axial section) [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)[[6]](/library/O9YInr)[[9]](/library/-bbDwH)




* Indication: imaging modality of choice  [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)[[6]](/library/O9YInr)[[9]](/library/-bbDwH)

* Characteristic findings 

* Enlargement of the <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>psoas</u> muscle

* Well-defined <u>abscess</u>: encapsulated <u>hypodense</u> lesion with peripheral <u>enhancement</u>, with or without gas shadows, within the <u>psoas</u> muscle

* Signs of an intraabdominal or <u>pelvic</u> primary focus on infection, if present (e.g. <u>peritoneal</u> <u>fat stranding</u> adjacent to inflamed bowel, destruction of the <u>vertebral body</u> in <u>vertebral osteomyelitis</u>)

#### <u>MRI</u> of the <u>pelvis</u> and abdomen with IV contrast [[9]](/library/-bbDwH)




* Indications

* Suspected <u>psoas</u> <u>abscess</u> in a patient with <u>contraindications for CT</u> scan

* Suspected spinal pathology and evaluation of <u>back pain</u> [[6]](/library/O9YInr)

* Consider <u>MR enterography</u> if <u>Crohn disease</u> is suspected to be the underlying etiology. [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)

* Pregnant women: <u>MRI</u> without contrast is preferred

* Characteristic findings

* Similar to those in CT

* <u>Abscess</u>: <u>hypointense</u> in T1, <u>hyperintense</u> in T2





#### Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> [[10]](/library/k9Ymnr)




* Indications

* An alternative to <u>MRI</u> in patients with <u>contraindications for CT</u> scan

* May be used as a first-line imaging modality to evaluation for intraabdominal infection

* Supportive findings

* Asymmetrical swelling of the <u>psoas</u> muscle

* The <u>abscess</u> appears as a <u>hypoechoic</u> collection within the <u>psoas</u> muscle.

* Signs of intra-abdominal or <u>pelvic</u> primary focus





#### Imaging to evaluate for a suspected primary focus




A primary focus within the abdomen or <u>spine</u> may be discovered incidentally during the workup for <u>psoas</u> <u>abscess</u>.



* Consider the following:

* <u>MRI</u> of the <u>spine</u> in suspected <u>vertebral osteomyelitis</u>

* Imaging of the hip or knee in suspected <u>prosthetic joint infection</u> [[11]](/library/J-Ysy7)

* <u>TTE</u>/<u>TEE</u> in suspected <u>infective endocarditis</u>

* <u>Chest x-ray</u> in suspected pulmonary focus (e.g., <u>tuberculosis</u>)




> [!TIP]
> If no primary focus of infection can be identified, <u>primary psoas abscess</u> is most likely. [[7]](/library/PYbW6H)

---

## Treatment

### General principles [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)[[6]](/library/O9YInr)[[13]](/library/fyYke7)




* <u>Antibiotic therapy</u> and drainage of the <u>abscess</u> are the mainstays of therapy.

* Consider a trial of <u>antibiotic therapy</u> alone in small <u>abscesses</u> (< 3.5 cm). [[12]](/library/m9YVLr)[[13]](/library/fyYke7)

* <u>Abscess</u> drainage (either image-guided or surgical) is indicated in <u>septic</u> patients or if the <u>abscess</u> is large or multiloculated.

* Identify and treat the underlying condition (e.g., <u>appendectomy</u> in <u>appendicitis</u>; <u>tuberculosis therapy</u> if <u>tuberculosis</u> is confirmed)





### Empiric antibiotic therapy for psoas abscess [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)[[6]](/library/O9YInr)[[14]](/library/6-Yjy7)




* Coverage: empiric therapy should provide coverage of <u>S. aureus</u> and <u>E. coli</u>.

* Suggested regimens 

* One of the following <u>beta-lactams</u> with <u>beta-lactamase inhibitor</u>:

* <u>Ampicillin-sulbactam</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Piperacillin-tazobactam</u> DOSAGE

* OR combination therapy with <u>metronidazole</u> DOSAGE PLUS one of the following:

* A <u>third-generation cephalosporin</u> (e.g., <u>ceftriaxone</u> DOSAGE)

* A <u>fluoroquinolone</u> (e.g., <u>levofloxacin</u> DOSAGE)

* PLUS consider one of the following for <u>MRSA</u> coverage :

* <u>Vancomycin</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Linezolid</u> DOSAGE

* Additional considerations

* Tailor <u>antibiotic therapy</u> to culture <u>sensitivity</u> reports when they are available.

* Switch to oral <u>antibiotics</u> once the patient is afebrile.

* Duration of <u>antibiotic therapy</u>: usually 4–6 weeks  [[15]](/library/XXb99H)





### <u>Abscess</u> drainage




#### <u>Image-guided percutaneous drainage</u> (PCD)




* Indications

* Size of the <u>abscess</u> > 3.5 cm  [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)[[12]](/library/m9YVLr)[[13]](/library/fyYke7)

* <u>Abscess</u> anatomically amenable to PCD

* Procedure

* Under image guidance, drain the <u>abscess</u> and place the drainage catheter in the <u>abscess</u> cavity to allow further drainage.

* CT-guided drainage is preferred. [[12]](/library/m9YVLr)

* <u>Ultrasound</u>-guided drainage may be attempted if experienced radiologists are available.  [[10]](/library/k9Ymnr)





#### Surgical drainage




* Indications

* Multiloculated <u>abscesses</u>

* Catheters repeatedly blocked by thick <u>pus</u>

* <u>Abscess</u> inaccessible to percutaneous drainage

* <u>Septic shock</u> or <u>sepsis</u> not responding to <u>antibiotic therapy</u>

* Primary source of infection requires surgical management  [[2]](/library/-wYDlr)

* Procedure: open <u>surgery</u> or <u>laparoscopic</u> drainage





> [!TIP]
> Send <u>abscess</u> fluid for culture and tailor <u>antibiotic therapy</u> to the <u>sensitivity</u> reports.
